sketches.title: Loophole Lottery
sketches.premise: A real country has passed a painfully dull law. Turn its ordinary rule into a wild legal loophole without making the rule stop being true. The law stays on the books; your imagination gets to commit the misdemeanor.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that the card's law still reads as true in the move, while scoring how far the move travels into a clever, surprising loophole.
sketches.move_shape: Write one loophole claim under 90 characters that keeps the law true; invented cases, motives and consequences are fair game. Example: Card: “In Norway, shops must offer receipts.” Move: “Norway’s receipt law creates a black market for proof you bought nothing.”
sketches.first_card: In Japan, cars must have a safety inspection.

sketches.title: Fine-Print Fiasco
sketches.premise: Each card names a real country rule that sounds harmless until a lawyer starts poking it with a stick. Add one legal exception, demand or consequence that makes the rule dramatically worse while leaving its core intact. Congratulations: you found the sentence that ruins everyone’s day.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that the named rule remains true and scores the distance created by the added legal detail.
sketches.move_shape: Write a single mock legal notice under 90 characters, preserving the rule and adding a twist. Example: Card: “In Germany, Sunday shop closing is common.” Move: “Sunday shoppers may browse, but the bread must be purchased by Friday.”
sketches.first_card: In France, workers have a legal right to disconnect from work emails.

sketches.title: Ministerial Meltdown
sketches.premise: A country’s boring law has landed on a minister’s desk. Announce the official reason, emergency plan or public scandal behind it, but do not erase the law itself. Make the government sound either brilliantly prepared or spectacularly doomed.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that the card's law remains true and scores how wildly the invented government story expands around it.
sketches.move_shape: Write one official statement under 90 characters that keeps the law in force. Example: Card: “In Finland, some fishing rights are regulated.” Move: “The Fisheries Minister denies this is revenge for the trout-party incident.”
sketches.first_card: In New Zealand, voting is not compulsory.

sketches.title: Lawyer Says No
sketches.premise: You are a lawyer explaining a real country’s dull law to a client who wants to do something ridiculous. Give a sharp refusal, warning or loophole-free answer that still accepts the law as true. The client may be innocent, guilty or merely an absolute pain in the arse.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that the law stays true and scores how far the lawyer’s answer pushes the situation beyond the card.
sketches.move_shape: Write one lawyer-to-client line under 90 characters, keeping the law intact. Example: Card: “In Singapore, chewing gum sales are restricted.” Move: “No, Kevin, calling it ‘chewable wall putty’ will not fool customs.”
sketches.first_card: In Iceland, parents may choose a baby's given name from an approved list.

sketches.title: Two-Noun Statute
sketches.premise: Every card gives you two nouns from a real country’s law: an ordinary object and an ordinary person, place or group. Connect them with a new legal rule that keeps the card’s fact true. Make the pairing sound official, nasty or weirdly sensible.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that both card nouns remain meaningfully present and that the original legal fact is not contradicted, then scores the boldness of the connection.
sketches.move_shape: Write one statute-like sentence under 90 characters using both nouns and preserving the card’s law. Example: Card: “Canada: beaver; hat.” Move: “A beaver may not wear a hat while testifying before Parliament.”
sketches.first_card: Australia: kangaroo; road. In Australia, drivers must obey wildlife road signs.

sketches.title: Courtroom Callback
sketches.premise: A host reads a dull, checkable law from a real country, then asks for a courtroom line about it. Your line must leave the law true but turn the judge, witness or evidence into comedy. The gavel falls hardest on anyone who merely repeats the card.
sketches.criterion: The judge checks that the card's law remains true and scores how far the courtroom line transforms the two named nouns into a sharp legal moment.
sketches.move_shape: Write one courtroom line under 90 characters containing both card nouns; add any invented testimony, motive or insult. Example: Card: “Spain: siesta; worker.” Move: “The worker requests a siesta; the prosecutor calls it a paid nap with delusions.”
sketches.first_card: Switzerland: dog; tax. In Switzerland, some municipalities charge a tax on owning a dog.
